source_title: COMEX Hours: When Gold, Silver, and Copper Futures Trade
instrument: GC / XAUUSD (COMEX gold futures and spot-equivalent)
original_claim_summary: COMEX gold futures trade nearly 23 hours per weekday with a daily halt from 5:00-6:00 PM ET; outside the London-morning-to-US-afternoon window, market depth thins and price moves happen on reduced volume.
claimed_mechanism: During the daily 5-6pm ET trading halt and in low-participation windows (late Asia / very early European hours), fewer resting orders sit in the book, so the same order size causes a larger price move and a wider bid-ask spread than during the London/New York overlap.
context: Applies to the daily COMEX/Globex electronic session structure for gold futures, Sunday 6pm ET through Friday 5pm ET.
event_sequence: EVENT A: clock reaches the 5-6pm ET daily halt or a historically low-volume window -> transition: order-book depth falls -> EVENT B: realized spread widens and price impact per contract rises versus the London/NY overlap.
trigger: Time of day (daily maintenance break or off-peak session window)
invalidation: A high-impact scheduled news release or geopolitical shock occurring inside the normally thin window, which can produce deep liquidity despite the clock time
claimed_outcome: Wider spreads and choppier, lower-conviction price action outside the London-morning-to-US-daytime overlap; tighter, more directional pricing inside it
falsification_condition: If measured realized spread and price-impact-per-contract during the 5-6pm ET halt window or the Asia off-peak window were statistically equal to or tighter than spread/impact during the London-NY overlap across a representative multi-month sample, the claim would be false.

source_title: COMEX Hours: When Gold, Silver, and Copper Futures Trade
instrument: GC / XAUUSD (COMEX gold futures and spot-equivalent)
original_claim_summary: Metals liquidity is described as intensifying specifically during the London morning through the US daytime, i.e. a loosely defined late-morning-to-early-afternoon Eastern Time window, when both major financial centers are simultaneously active.
claimed_mechanism: Concurrent participation of European and US institutional desks in the same clock window increases simultaneous order flow, deepening the order book and narrowing spreads relative to single-center sessions.
context: Weekday gold futures/spot trading, comparing single-center sessions (Asia-only, London-only) against the London/NY overlap.
event_sequence: EVENT A: only one financial center is active (e.g. Asia session) -> transition: a second center (London, then New York) opens and overlaps -> EVENT B: order flow and book depth increase, spreads compress, directional moves become more decisive.
trigger: Clock entering the London/New York overlap window
invalidation: A holiday closure in one of the two centers (e.g. a UK or US bank holiday) that removes the expected overlap liquidity despite the clock window
claimed_outcome: Deeper liquidity, tighter execution, and cleaner directional price action during the overlap window versus single-session periods
falsification_condition: If measured trade count, quoted depth, or effective spread during the stated overlap window were not measurably better (deeper/tighter) than during non-overlapping single-center hours across a representative sample, the claim would be false.

source_title: Stylized facts of intraday precious metals
original_claim_summary: Using 15 years (2000-2015) of 5-minute gold price data, the study finds trading volume follows an n-shaped intraday pattern, peaking roughly 11am-5pm GMT while both European and North American markets are open.
claimed_mechanism: Gold trading volume rises through the morning, peaks while London and New York sessions overlap, and falls off after the European close, producing a hump-shaped (n-shaped) volume curve across the 24-hour cycle.
context: Global spot/OTC gold market, 5-minute bars, 2000-2015 sample, measured in GMT.
event_sequence: EVENT A: Asia/early-London hours with below-average volume -> transition: London and New York sessions both become active (approx. 11am-5pm GMT) -> EVENT B: volume rises to its daily peak, then declines after the European close.
trigger: Time of day crossing into the 11am-5pm GMT window
invalidation: A sample period or subperiod in which the volume curve is flat or bimodal rather than single-peaked n-shaped
claimed_outcome: An n-shaped (single hump) intraday volume curve for gold, peaking during the London/New York overlap
falsification_condition: If an intraday volume profile computed over a comparable long sample of gold 5-minute data showed a flat, bimodal, or inverse (u-shaped) pattern instead of a single peak during the London/NY overlap, the claim would be false.

source_title: Stylized facts of intraday precious metals
original_claim_summary: Gold realized volatility is described as fairly flat until roughly 12pm GMT, rises modestly to a local peak near 2pm GMT, then decreases and flattens for the remainder of the day.
claimed_mechanism: Realized 5-minute volatility in gold shows a modest, not extreme, intraday cycle: a rise concentrated around the US data/equity-open window (12pm-2pm GMT) rather than a dramatic spike-and-collapse pattern.
context: Global gold market, 2000-2015, 5-minute bar realized volatility measured in GMT.
event_sequence: EVENT A: volatility near its flat overnight/morning baseline (pre-12pm GMT) -> transition: US pre-market data releases and equity open occur (12pm-2pm GMT) -> EVENT B: volatility rises to a local peak near 2pm GMT then decays through the rest of the day.
trigger: Time of day approaching 12pm-2pm GMT (US data/open window)
invalidation: A volatility profile that is flat all day or peaks at a different, unrelated time (e.g. only during the Asia session)
claimed_outcome: A modest, single-peaked intraday volatility cycle for gold centered near 2pm GMT
falsification_condition: If realized volatility computed on the same 5-minute gold data showed no statistically distinguishable rise around 12pm-2pm GMT relative to the rest of the day, the claim would be false.

source_title: Stylized facts of intraday precious metals
original_claim_summary: In contrast to the strong intraday spread cycles seen in some other markets, the study reports gold's quoted bid-ask spread stays fairly constant across the trading day, with only minor widening around the daily close.
claimed_mechanism: Unlike instruments with pronounced open/close spread spikes, gold's quoted spread in the 2000-2015 sample does not systematically widen during Asia hours or narrow only during the London/NY overlap; it is roughly flat with a small bump near the daily market close.
context: Global gold market, institutional quoted spreads (Thomson Reuters), 2000-2015, 5-minute resolution.
event_sequence: EVENT A: any time of day outside the daily close window -> EVENT B: spread stays within a narrow, roughly constant band; a small widening appears only near the market's daily close.
trigger: Approach of the daily market close
invalidation: A finding (e.g. from retail broker spread data) showing large, session-dependent spread swings (tight in overlap, much wider in Asia) that contradict the flat institutional-quote pattern
claimed_outcome: Roughly constant intraday bid-ask spread for gold at the institutional quote level, with only a minor close-time widening
falsification_condition: If gold's quoted spread showed a large, statistically significant session-dependent cycle (e.g. multiple times wider in Asia hours than in the London/NY overlap) rather than a roughly flat profile, the claim would be false. Note: this finding may not hold for retail broker markup spreads, which are a different measurement than institutional quoted spread.

source_title: Stylized facts of intraday precious metals
original_claim_summary: The study reports statistically significant periodicity in gold returns tied to the opening and closing times of major regional markets (Asia, Europe, US), rather than returns being uniformly random across the trading day.
claimed_mechanism: Average 5-minute returns show recurring, time-of-day-specific patterns clustered around the open/close clock times of the Asia, European, and US markets, rather than being independent of clock time.
context: Global gold market, 2000-2015, 5-minute return periodicity measured relative to regional market open/close times.
event_sequence: EVENT A: clock time approaches a regional market's stated open or close -> EVENT B: average 5-minute returns around that clock time deviate from the all-day average in a statistically detectable, recurring way.
trigger: Clock time coinciding with a regional market open/close
invalidation: A finding that 5-minute average returns are statistically indistinguishable from random noise regardless of proximity to market opens/closes
claimed_outcome: Detectable, recurring return periodicity tied to global market open/close times
falsification_condition: If a formal periodicity test (e.g. ANOVA or spectral test) on 5-minute gold returns found no statistically significant clustering around regional open/close times after correcting for multiple comparisons, the claim would be false.

source_title: Intraday Seasonality in Efficiency, Liquidity, Volatility and Volume: Platinum and Gold Futures in Tokyo and New York
author_if_known: Kentaro Iwatsubo, Clinton Watkins, Tao Xu
instrument: Gold futures (TOCOM Tokyo and COMEX New York)
timeframe: intraday (session-level, published in Journal of Commodity Markets 2018)
original_claim_summary: Comparing Tokyo and New York trading-day sessions for the same underlying gold futures, the study finds Tokyo session activity is dominated by uninformed (liquidity) trading, while the New York day session shows evidence of both uninformed and informed trading.
claimed_mechanism: When gold futures trade on the Tokyo exchange during Tokyo day hours, order flow behaves more like liquidity-driven (non-directional-information) trading; when the same underlying trades on COMEX during New York day hours, order flow shows measurable informed-trading characteristics (price impact patterns consistent with participants trading on private information), indicating the two sessions have different microstructure even for the same commodity.
context: Cross-exchange comparison of gold futures, Tokyo day session vs. New York day session, using standard market-microstructure informed/uninformed trading proxies.
event_sequence: EVENT A: gold futures trade during the Tokyo day session -> observed microstructure: dominated by liquidity/uninformed flow. EVENT B (separate session): the same underlying trades during the New York day session -> observed microstructure: informed-trading signatures present alongside liquidity flow.
trigger: Session/venue identity (Tokyo day session vs. New York day session)
invalidation: Finding no measurable difference in informed-vs-uninformed trading proxies between the Tokyo and New York gold futures sessions
claimed_outcome: Distinct microstructure regimes for gold futures depending on which regional session/venue is active, implying informed traders concentrate activity in the New York window
falsification_condition: If standard informed-trading proxies (e.g. price-impact-of-volume regressions) computed separately on Tokyo-hour and New York-hour gold futures data showed no significant difference between the two sessions, the claim would be false.

source_title: Intraday Seasonality in Efficiency, Liquidity, Volatility and Volume: Platinum and Gold Futures in Tokyo and New York
author_if_known: Kentaro Iwatsubo, Clinton Watkins, Tao Xu
instrument: Gold futures (TOCOM Tokyo and COMEX New York)
original_claim_summary: The paper argues traders self-select which session to trade in based on the prevailing microstructure characteristics of that session, implying gold futures markets on different exchanges (same underlying commodity) develop persistently different liquidity/informational profiles rather than converging to one global norm.
claimed_mechanism: Because Tokyo trading in gold futures is structurally dominated by liquidity flow while New York day-session trading shows more informed-trading signatures, market participants with different objectives (hedgers/liquidity traders vs. information-driven traders) route their activity to the session whose microstructure suits them, reinforcing the split rather than eroding it over time.
context: Cross-exchange gold futures market structure; applies to the stable, recurring venue-level microstructure difference rather than any single day's anomaly.
event_sequence: EVENT A: a trading desk with a directional information edge chooses when/where to route gold futures orders -> transition: order is placed preferentially in the New York day session -> EVENT B: New York session microstructure continues to show more informed-trading signatures than Tokyo, persistently.
invalidation: Evidence that the Tokyo/New York microstructure gap for gold futures has closed or reversed over an extended recent sample
claimed_outcome: Persistent, non-converging differences in gold futures microstructure across exchanges/sessions due to self-selected order routing
falsification_condition: If a more recent sample of gold futures data showed the Tokyo/New York informed-vs-uninformed trading gap narrowing toward zero or reversing direction, the self-selection/persistence claim would be false.

source_title: How XAUUSD liquidity mapping works
original_claim_summary: The broker article describes a recurring three-stage sequence around key XAUUSD reference levels (prior day/week highs-lows, equal highs/lows, round numbers, trendlines): price first pierces the level (sweep), then trades sideways (accumulation/distribution), then makes a strong directional move away from the level (displacement), and states the post-sweep reaction matters more than the sweep itself.
claimed_mechanism: Price briefly trades beyond a well-known reference level (prior day/week high or low, an area of repeated equal highs/lows, a round number, or a trendline) where resting stop orders are concentrated, then consolidates in a sideways range near that level, and finally produces a large, fast candle moving away from the level in one direction.
context: XAUUSD price approaching a widely-watched reference level where retail stop orders are assumed to cluster.
prerequisite_state: Price approaching or briefly exceeding a previous day/week high or low, an equal-highs/lows zone, a round number, or a trendline
event_sequence: EVENT A: price sweeps beyond the reference level -> transition: price consolidates sideways near the level (accumulation/distribution) -> EVENT B: a large displacement candle moves price away from the level in the resolved direction.
trigger: Sideways consolidation resolving with a large expansion candle away from the swept level
invalidation: Price sweeps the level but instead of consolidating and displacing away, continues to trend strongly through the level without any sideways pause
claimed_outcome: A directional move away from the swept reference level, following a consolidation phase
falsification_condition: If, across a systematic sample of XAUUSD sweeps of prior day/week highs-lows, the subsequent consolidation-then-displacement sequence occurred no more often than chance (e.g. displacement direction is unpredictable from the sweep+consolidation pattern), the claim would be false.

source_title: How XAUUSD liquidity mapping works
original_claim_summary: The article identifies specific XAUUSD price zones where retail stop orders concentrate: previous daily and weekly highs/lows, areas of repeated equal highs/lows, round psychological numbers (e.g. $3000, $4000, $5000), and price levels just beyond commonly-drawn trendlines.
claimed_mechanism: Because many retail traders place stop-loss or breakout orders just beyond the same visually obvious reference points (prior day/week extremes, repeated equal highs/lows, round numbers, trendlines), those specific price zones accumulate an above-average concentration of resting orders compared to arbitrary nearby price levels.
context: XAUUSD price approaching widely-observed chart reference levels.
prerequisite_state: A prior day/week high or low, a repeated equal-high/low zone, a round number, or a trendline exists nearby on the chart
event_sequence: EVENT A: price approaches one of these reference zones -> EVENT B: an above-average cluster of stop/breakout orders is triggered as price reaches or slightly exceeds the zone.
trigger: Price reaching within a small distance of the reference level
invalidation: Order-flow or level-2 data showing no measurable increase in triggered stop volume at these levels relative to random nearby price points
claimed_outcome: Elevated order execution/triggering activity precisely at these specific chart levels
falsification_condition: If broker- or exchange-level order-flow data showed no statistically elevated concentration of stop/breakout order execution at prior day/week highs-lows, equal-highs/lows zones, or round numbers compared to randomly chosen nearby price levels, the claim would be false.

source_title: Why the Gold-Dollar Rule Fails — and What Works Instead
original_claim_summary: The author argues that gold's typical inverse relationship with the US Dollar Index (DXY) breaks down during acute risk-off/crisis events, when both gold and the dollar rise together as investors seek safety broadly (citing March 2020 and 2008 as examples).
claimed_mechanism: In most conditions, DXY strength coincides with gold weakness and vice versa; but during a sudden, broad flight-to-safety shock, both the dollar (as a safe-haven currency) and gold (as a safe-haven asset) can rise simultaneously, so a rule that treats DXY moves as automatically inverse to gold gives a wrong signal specifically during acute crisis windows.
context: Acute financial-market stress or crisis events (e.g. March 2020 COVID shock, 2008 financial crisis) versus normal market regimes.
prerequisite_state: An acute, broad-based risk-off shock is underway across asset classes
event_sequence: EVENT A: a systemic shock triggers simultaneous safe-haven demand for both USD and gold -> EVENT B: DXY and gold rise together, contradicting the typical inverse-correlation assumption.
trigger: Onset of an acute, broad-based flight-to-safety event
invalidation: The normal inverse DXY-gold relationship reasserting itself even during a labeled crisis period
claimed_outcome: Simultaneous DXY and gold appreciation during crisis windows, defeating a mechanical inverse-correlation trading rule
falsification_condition: If a systematic study of rolling DXY-gold correlation around historical acute crisis windows showed the correlation remaining reliably negative (rather than flipping positive or near zero) during those windows, the claim would be false.

source_title: Why the Gold-Dollar Rule Fails — and What Works Instead
instrument: XAUUSD vs. US 10-year TIPS real yield
original_claim_summary: The author proposes replacing DXY with the US 10-year TIPS (real) yield as the primary gold driver, arguing gold can rise even against a strong nominal dollar when real yields are falling or deeply negative, citing 2020-2022 and late 2023-early 2024 as examples.
claimed_mechanism: Because gold pays no yield, its opportunity cost is set by real (inflation-adjusted) interest rates rather than by the nominal dollar index; when the 10-year TIPS yield falls or turns deeply negative, gold becomes relatively more attractive and tends to rise even if DXY is flat or rising.
context: Periods of falling or deeply negative US real interest rates, regardless of concurrent DXY direction.
prerequisite_state: US 10-year TIPS yield is falling or already deeply negative
event_sequence: EVENT A: 10-year TIPS real yield declines or sits deeply negative -> EVENT B: gold price rises (or holds up) even when DXY is stable or strengthening.
trigger: A sustained decline in the 10-year TIPS yield
invalidation: Gold falling or failing to rally during a period of falling/deeply negative real yields, or gold's move tracking DXY more closely than real yields during such a period
claimed_outcome: Gold price direction tracks real yield direction more reliably than it tracks the nominal dollar index
falsification_condition: If a regression of gold returns on changes in the 10-year TIPS yield versus changes in DXY, over a multi-year sample, showed DXY explaining gold's direction better (or equally well) rather than real yields dominating, the claim would be false.

source_title: Best Liquidity Grab/Sweep Strategy For Trading Forex Gold
original_claim_summary: A valid daily-timeframe 'liquidity grab' on gold is defined as a candle whose wick pierces a marked supply/demand zone while its body stays inside the zone; after this, price is expected to consolidate into a lower-timeframe range whose breakout signals the trade direction.
claimed_mechanism: When a daily candle's wick extends beyond a previously marked support/resistance (supply/demand) zone but the candle's close (body) remains inside that zone, this indicates the breach was rejected rather than accepted; a subsequent sideways range on the 1H/4H chart that later breaks in one direction is used as the actual entry signal.
context: XAUUSD daily-chart supply/demand zones, confirmed with lower-timeframe (1H/4H) range formation.
prerequisite_state: A daily candle's wick has pierced a marked supply or demand zone while the candle's body closed back inside it
event_sequence: EVENT A: daily wick pierces the zone, body closes back inside (grab confirmed) -> transition: price consolidates into a horizontal range on 1H/4H -> EVENT B: price breaks the range in the direction implied by the grab, triggering entry on a retest of the broken range boundary.
trigger: 1H/4H range breakout following the daily-candle wick rejection
invalidation: The daily candle's body (not just the wick) closes beyond the zone, indicating acceptance rather than rejection of the breach
claimed_outcome: A directional move following the range breakout, with the source claiming an approximate 80% win rate when combined with multi-timeframe confirmation
falsification_condition: If a systematic backtest of this exact wick-only-violation-plus-range-breakout rule on historical XAUUSD daily/1H data produced a win rate no better than a naive random-direction baseline after costs, the claim (including the stated ~80% win rate) would be false.

source_title: CRT: Strict Three-Candle Framework
timeframe: not specified (candle-sequence based, applicable to any timeframe)
original_claim_summary: Describes 'Candle Range Theory' (CRT) as a strict three-candle sequence on gold: candle 1 sets a high/low range, candle 2 must immediately pierce one side of that range and close back inside it, and candle 3 is expected to move toward the opposite side of the range.
claimed_mechanism: The first candle's high and low define a reference range. The second candle must, without delay, trade beyond one boundary of that range and then close back inside it (a brief overshoot-and-reject); any candle that instead closes outside the range, or that only sweeps after a delay, invalidates the pattern. The third candle is expected to move away from the side that was swept, toward the opposite boundary of the original range.
context: Any XAUUSD chart where a clear prior-candle range exists, most commonly applied on H1-H4.
prerequisite_state: A defined benchmark candle (candle 1) whose high/low form the reference range
event_sequence: EVENT A (candle 1): a range is established -> EVENT B (candle 2, immediately following): price pierces one boundary of the range intrabar but closes back inside it -> EVENT C (candle 3): price moves directionally toward the opposite boundary of the original range.
trigger: Candle 2 closing back inside the range after piercing one boundary
invalidation: Candle 2's body closes outside the range (breach accepted, not rejected); the sweep does not occur immediately after candle 1 (extra candles trapped inside the range first)
claimed_outcome: Price delivers toward the opposite boundary of the original range following the reject-and-close-back-inside candle
falsification_condition: If a systematic scan of XAUUSD historical bars for this exact three-candle sequence (range, immediate wick-reject, close-back-inside) found that candle 3 moved toward the opposite boundary no more often than toward the same side (i.e. no better than chance), the claim would be false.

source_title: ICT Breaker Blocks: A Guide to Trading Failed Order Blocks
timeframe: not specified (general SMC/ICT concept, applicable to any instrument including XAUUSD)
original_claim_summary: Describes a 'breaker block' as a prior swing high/low that price briefly exceeds (a stop-hunt/liquidity sweep) and then, via a large fast candle closing beyond that swing point, flips into a new support/resistance zone; entries are placed at the 50% midpoint of the breaking candle's body.
claimed_mechanism: A prior swing high or low that many traders treat as a reversal point is instead exceeded briefly (price wicks through it, triggering stops resting beyond it). Immediately afterward, one or more large, fast-moving candles close decisively beyond that same swing point without much pullback. That combination (brief overshoot + decisive close-through) flips the old swing zone into a new support/resistance area; a limit order is then placed at the midpoint of the price range of the candle that produced the decisive close.
context: Any market/instrument where a recent swing high/low has just been briefly exceeded and then a strong, fast move continues in the breach direction, ideally aligned with the higher-timeframe trend.
prerequisite_state: A recent swing high/low exists and price has just wicked beyond it (liquidity sweep) before a strong displacement move
event_sequence: EVENT A: a swing high/low forms -> EVENT B: price briefly wicks beyond that swing point (sweep) -> EVENT C: one or more large, fast candles close decisively beyond the same point (displacement), flipping it into new support/resistance -> entry placed at the 50% level of the displacement candle's body on a retest.
trigger: Price retesting the 50% (mean threshold) level of the displacement candle's body after the flip
invalidation: Price retraces back through and closes beyond the wick of the original liquidity-sweep candle, which the source states means 'the institutional narrative has changed'
claimed_outcome: Price respects the flipped zone as new support/resistance and moves further in the breakout direction from the 50% retest
falsification_condition: If a systematic scan for this exact sequence (swing point, brief wick-through, decisive displacement close-through, retest of the 50% body level) found the subsequent move continued in the displacement direction no more often than it reversed, across a representative multi-instrument sample, the claim would be false.

source_title: ICT Breaker Blocks: A Guide to Trading Failed Order Blocks
original_claim_summary: States that a breaker-block setup requires the liquidity sweep to be validated by a subsequent market-structure shift with displacement; drift above/below the level without a fast, energetic candle does not qualify, and higher-timeframe alignment toward unmitigated liquidity is required for the setup to be considered valid.
claimed_mechanism: Two specific filters are required before treating a swept swing point as tradeable: (1) the move away from the swept level must be a large, fast candle (not a slow grind), and (2) the direction must point toward a nearby untested prior high/low on a higher timeframe. Absent either condition, the same price pattern (sweep + some follow-through) is not considered a valid breaker.
context: Filtering which liquidity sweeps are considered tradeable breaker-block setups versus which are not.
prerequisite_state: A liquidity sweep of a swing high/low has occurred
event_sequence: EVENT A: swing point is swept -> check 1: does a large, fast candle close beyond the level (displacement) rather than a slow drift? -> check 2: does the implied direction point toward an unmitigated higher-timeframe liquidity target? -> only if both checks pass is the setup treated as valid.
trigger: Presence of a fast displacement candle plus higher-timeframe directional alignment
invalidation: Price drifts slowly beyond the level without a fast displacement candle, or the direction does not align with a higher-timeframe unmitigated level
claimed_outcome: Setups meeting both filters are implied to perform better (are 'high probability') than sweeps failing either filter, though no comparative statistic is given
falsification_condition: If sweeps followed by slow drift (no displacement candle) performed no worse than sweeps followed by a fast displacement candle in a systematic forward test, the claimed filter would add no value and the claim would be false.

source_title: Liquidity Sweep vs Liquidity Run
original_claim_summary: Distinguishes two outcomes when price reaches a prior equal-high/low or swing level: a 'sweep' (wick prints through, close prints back inside, followed by reversal) versus a 'run' (price captures the level and keeps moving the same direction, without returning). It proposes that alignment with higher-timeframe direction predicts which outcome occurs.
claimed_mechanism: When price reaches a marked equal-high/low or swing level: if the candle's close prints back inside the prior range after only a brief wick beyond it, and a market-structure shift appears on a lower timeframe, a reversal (sweep) tends to follow. If instead price continues closing beyond the level with a strong momentum move away from the prior range (displacement, no return to the origin), a continuation (run) tends to follow. The source claims the higher-timeframe trend direction at the time predicts which of the two occurs: sweep against the higher-timeframe direction produces a reversal, sweep with the higher-timeframe direction produces a run.
context: Price interacting with a marked liquidity level (equal highs/lows or a swing point), assessed against the prevailing higher-timeframe directional bias.
prerequisite_state: A marked equal-high/low or prior swing level exists and price is approaching it; a higher-timeframe directional bias has been established
event_sequence: EVENT A: price reaches the marked level -> check: does price close back inside the range (sweep) or keep closing beyond it (run)? -> EVENT B: if higher-timeframe bias disagrees with the side just taken out, expect reversal (sweep); if higher-timeframe bias agrees, expect continuation (run).
trigger: Price reaching the marked level, filtered by higher-timeframe directional bias
invalidation: The higher-timeframe-bias rule failing to predict sweep-vs-run outcome better than chance across many instances
claimed_outcome: Reversal after sweeps that oppose the higher-timeframe bias; continuation after sweeps that align with it
falsification_condition: If, across a systematic sample of level-sweeps, the outcome (close-back-inside reversal vs. continued-close-through run) were unrelated to the prevailing higher-timeframe directional bias (i.e. predicted no better than a coin flip), the claim would be false.

source_title: Liquidity Sweep vs Liquidity Run
original_claim_summary: States that after identifying a liquidity sweep, entry should be taken on the retest of the price-delivery zone left behind after the close-back-inside, not on the initial wick, with a stop placed a few points beyond the swept level to avoid getting stopped out by a re-test of the wick.
claimed_mechanism: Rather than entering during the wick itself (which is a brief, hard-to-execute overshoot), the rule waits for price to close back inside the range and then return ('retest') to revisit the origin zone of that reversal before entering; the stop-loss sits beyond the extreme of the wick, not at the entry zone, to tolerate a shallow re-poke of the same wick without being stopped out.
context: Execution/entry-timing rule following an already-identified liquidity sweep and reversal.
prerequisite_state: A liquidity sweep (wick through level, close back inside) has already occurred
event_sequence: EVENT A: sweep occurs and price closes back inside the range -> transition: price pulls back to retest the origin zone of the reversal -> EVENT B: entry is taken on this retest, with stop placed beyond the sweep candle's wick.
trigger: Price retesting the origin zone after the initial close-back-inside
invalidation: Price never returns to retest the zone (moves away immediately), leaving no valid entry under this rule; or the wick is retaken beyond the placed stop level
claimed_outcome: A safer, better-priced entry than entering directly on the sweep wick, at the cost of sometimes missing the move if no retest occurs
falsification_condition: If retest-based entries after a confirmed sweep produced worse average outcomes (lower win rate or worse risk-adjusted return) than simply entering at the close-back-inside bar in a systematic backtest, the claimed benefit of waiting for the retest would be false.

source_title: Gold Trading Strategy: New York Open Range Breakout Scalping
original_claim_summary: Forum participants describe the New York session as offering more reliable, tradable gold price action than the London session, with the London session more often producing fakeouts that get reversed before the 'real' New York move develops; entries reportedly require confirming rejection candles and the speed/strength of the breakout move.
claimed_mechanism: A breakout of the New York opening range is treated as a valid continuation signal only when confirmed by two candles showing rejection of the opposite side (i.e. two consecutive candles failing to close back against the breakout direction) combined with visibly fast, strong momentum in the breakout candle(s); breakouts lacking this rejection/velocity confirmation are more likely to be false moves, similar to those commonly seen during the London session.
context: XAUUSD intraday trading around the New York cash/futures session open, contrasted against London-session breakout attempts.
prerequisite_state: Price has broken beyond the New York opening range
event_sequence: EVENT A: price breaks the New York opening range boundary -> check: do two subsequent candles reject the opposite side, and does the breakout show high velocity? -> EVENT B: if confirmed, treat as a valid continuation trade; if not, treat as a likely fakeout similar to typical London-session breakouts.
trigger: Two-candle rejection confirmation plus visible breakout velocity
invalidation: Breakout reverses back into the opening range shortly after triggering, or the two-candle rejection confirmation fails to materialize
claimed_outcome: New York opening-range breakouts confirmed by rejection candles and velocity are more reliable continuation trades than unconfirmed breakouts or typical London-session breakouts
claimed_horizon: intraday (minutes to a few hours post-open)
falsification_condition: If a systematic sample of New York opening-range breakouts on XAUUSD showed no difference in follow-through rate between breakouts with two-candle rejection confirmation and those without, or if London-session breakouts failed no more often than New York breakouts, the claim would be false.

source_title: Opening Range Breakout - A Century of Evidence
instrument: 84 futures markets across grains, softs, meats, metals, energies, currencies, rates, and equity indices (gold/metals not individually broken out in the excerpt reviewed)
timeframe: daily (opening range breakout, held to next day's open)
original_claim_summary: A buy/sell-stop opening range breakout rule (entering at 0.8x the prior ten-day range beyond the open, held to the next day's open with no protective stop) produced a positive Sharpe ratio (1.40) across 84 futures markets over 102 years (1923-2025), but the edge has decayed markedly in recent decades (2.92 in the 2000s, down to 0.91 in the 2010s).
claimed_mechanism: Placing a stop order to enter in the breakout direction once price moves 0.8 times the prior ten-day average daily range beyond today's opening price, then holding the position with no stop until the next day's open, produces a positive average return in aggregate across a large panel of futures markets, though this average edge has been shrinking decade over decade in the most recent data.
context: Diversified panel of 84 futures markets (not gold-specific in the material reviewed), 1923-2025, daily bars.
prerequisite_state: A ten-day average daily range has been computed to size the day's breakout trigger
event_sequence: EVENT A: today's open is established -> EVENT B: price moves 0.8x the 10-day average range beyond the open, triggering entry in that direction -> hold with no stop until the next day's open.
trigger: Price crossing 0.8x the 10-day range from today's open
invalidation: A market/decade combination where the strategy's average return is flat or negative rather than positive
claimed_outcome: A structurally positive but decaying long-run average edge for this simple opening-range-breakout rule across diversified futures markets
falsification_condition: If the same 0.8x-ten-day-range breakout rule, when isolated specifically to gold futures data across the full sample, produced a Sharpe ratio at or below zero rather than a positive figure, the claim of a broad-based structural edge would not hold for gold specifically (even if it held for the aggregate panel).

source_title: Structural Limits of OHLCV-Based Intraday Momentum Signals in MNQ Futures: A Systematic Falsification Study
original_claim_summary: The paper tests the plain-language version of the ICT 'liquidity sweep/grab' idea (price temporarily pierces a session extreme, then closes back inside) on 6,442 identified events in MNQ futures, and finds neither fading the sweep direction nor trading with it produces a statistically positive net return after realistic transaction costs (both T-statistics strongly negative, around -13 to -14).
claimed_mechanism: Price piercing a session high/low and closing back inside it (a liquidity sweep) does not, on its own, predict either a reversal (fading the sweep) or a continuation (trading with the sweep) on 5-minute bars once realistic round-trip friction is applied; the gross directional content around such sweeps (0.20-0.80 points) is smaller than the cost of executing the trade.
context: MNQ intraday index futures, Asia-session extreme sweeps identified systematically over 2022-2025 under walk-forward out-of-sample testing.
prerequisite_state: Price has pierced a session extreme (high or low) and closed back inside the prior range, forming an identified liquidity-sweep event
event_sequence: EVENT A: price pierces a session extreme -> EVENT B: price closes back inside the range (sweep confirmed) -> tested outcome: neither fading nor following this event produces a statistically positive net return after costs.
trigger: Confirmed liquidity-sweep event (pierce + close back inside)
invalidation: A version of this test with a positive, cost-adjusted, out-of-sample T-statistic above 2.0 in either direction
claimed_outcome: No tradable directional edge exists purely from the sweep-and-close-back-inside pattern at 5-minute bar-close execution once transaction costs are applied
falsification_condition: This claim (a negative/null finding) would itself be falsified if a comparable walk-forward, cost-adjusted test of the same sweep-and-close-back-inside pattern on MNQ or a similar liquid futures instrument produced a statistically significant positive net return (T >= 2.0) in a consistent direction across multiple out-of-sample years.

source_title: Structural Limits of OHLCV-Based Intraday Momentum Signals in MNQ Futures: A Systematic Falsification Study
original_claim_summary: An Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-style intraday mean-reversion signal was tested directly on Micro Gold Futures (MGC) 5-minute bars across multiple z-score thresholds and both long/short directions; every configuration produced a negative net return after instrument-appropriate transaction costs across 2023-2025.
claimed_mechanism: A statistical model assumes gold's intraday price reverts toward a rolling mean once it deviates by a given number of standard deviations (an OU/mean-reversion process); entering against the deviation (fading extended moves) at several threshold levels, on 5-minute MGC bars, produces a negative average return per trade once realistic round-trip costs (0.50 points) are subtracted, in every tested configuration and year.
context: Micro Gold Futures (MGC), 5-minute intraday data, 2023-2025 (2025 partial), threshold-based mean-reversion entries.
prerequisite_state: Price has deviated from its rolling mean by more than the tested z-score threshold (1.5 or 2.0)
event_sequence: EVENT A: MGC 5-minute price deviates beyond the threshold from its rolling mean -> EVENT B: a mean-reversion trade is entered against the deviation -> tested outcome: average net return after costs is negative across all thresholds, directions, and years tested.
trigger: Price crossing the specified z-score deviation threshold from its rolling mean
invalidation: A version of the test with a positive net-of-cost average return for at least one threshold/direction combination, consistent across years
claimed_outcome: Intraday mean-reversion fading of extended gold-futures moves is not profitable after realistic costs at any of the tested thresholds
falsification_condition: This negative finding would be falsified if a comparable walk-forward, cost-adjusted OU mean-reversion test on MGC (or closely related gold futures) 5-minute data produced a statistically positive, cost-adjusted net return in a consistent direction across multiple out-of-sample years.
